newsitem.title: UK: British election opens in sunshine, tight security.
newsitem.headline: British election opens in sunshine, tight security.

text.p: Britons began voting in a landmark election on Thursday which looked set to end 18 years of Conservative party rule that transformed the country.
Opinion polls predict the opposition Labour party of Tony Blair will win a resounding victory over the ruling party of Prime Minister John Major.
The polls gave Major no chance in the 1992 election, which he won by 21 seats. The polls also say that many of Britain's 44 million voters have yet to make up their minds how to vote.
"I have not contemplated anything other than winning. I have a very positive attitude to this campaign," said Major, who succeeded Margaret Thatcher in 1990, in one of his last interviews.
The sun was shining brightly over much of the country and the BBC reported long queues outside some of the 45,000 polling stations before they opened.

Security was increased amid fears the banned Irish Republican Army (IRA), which wants end British rule in Northern Ireland, might try to disrupt proceedings. Voters were warned that their bags might be searched.
The IRA sparked chaos several times in the six-week campaign by planting small bombs on major motorways and making hoax calls which forced the closure of airports and railway stations.
The Home Office (interior ministry) last week sent leaflets to returning officers advising them how to cope with bomb threats. If necessary, voting in affected areas will be continued on Friday.

Opinion polls in Thursday's newspapers gave Labour leads of between 10 points and 22 points. If true, this could result in a landslide for Blair, who has dragged his party into the centre of the political spectrum since taking over in 1994.
But Labour has consistently said its own surveys suggest a much narrower gap between the two main parties and to the very end Blair warned against complacency.
If the Conservatives do win, it will be the biggest political upset since 1945, when Britons ousted wartime prime minister Winston Churchill and elected Labour with a landslide.
A win for Blair, 43, will earn him the title of Britain's youngest prime minister this century in succession to Major.
The tabloid Sun newspaper, which claimed its relentless assaults on Labour won the 1992 election for the Conservatives, switched sides some weeks ago.
Thursday's front page showed Blair's smiling face with a sparkling finger pointing to it and the caption "It must be you" in a take-off of the adverts for Britain's national lottery.
Blair ditched some of Labour's key socialist tenets, winning the support of business leaders alarmed by old Labour's links to the unions and reputation for high taxes and profligacy.
Labour finance spokesman Gordon Brown has pledged not to raise personal taxes for the life of the next parliament and has vowed to keep tight control on public spending.

The Conservatives, who stand to win an unprecedented fifth term of office if elected, argue they are the only party with the experience to run Britain. Their campaign posters read "Britain Is Booming, Don't Let Labour Blow It."
But Major has spent most of his campaign on the backfoot, battling the allegations of sleaze and the divisions over Europe that have dogged his party for most of the last five years.
In the middle of the campaign, he was forced into an emergency broadcast, appealing to voters to disregard the views of rebellious politicians opposed to closer links to the European Union.
